title: Can Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act be Reliably Identified in Email Messages?
research_question: Can human annotators reliably and repeatedly identify the presence and strength of requests for action and commitments to act in workplace email at sentence level well enough to support later automated classification?
methodology: The exploratory study manually selected 54 messages containing 310 sentences from a random subset of the Enron Email Corpus, deliberately seeking varied explicit and implicit requests, commitments, and task addressivity while restricting messages to fewer than 12 sentences. Three coders, who were also the paper's authors, independently annotated each sentence for the presence and Strong, Medium, Weak, or None strength of Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act, with audience type and processing-error flags also recorded. Agreement was measured with pairwise and three-way generalized kappa, and disagreement cases were qualitatively analyzed to identify recurring sources of ambiguity.

key_findings.finding: Annotators agreed relatively well on whether a sentence contained a Request-for-Action, with three-way kappa 0.78, but agreement on request strength was lower at 0.60.
Commitments-to-Act were substantially harder to annotate: presence achieved three-way kappa 0.54 and strength only 0.37.
Agreement varied with audience type and was highest for single-recipient messages and lowest for closed-group messages, with the effect particularly pronounced for commitments.
Conditional offers were a major systematic ambiguity: sentences containing offers accounted for almost 40% of disagreements about whether a Commitment-to-Act was present.
Implicit requests, especially meeting-related statements, produced recurring disagreement because identifying the obligation can require information from other parts of the message.

Missing organizational relationship information created ambiguity in judging request and commitment strength, with coders noting that the same wording could differ depending on whether the sender was a manager or a peer.
Coder error flags suggested at least a 10% sentence-segmentation error rate on the pilot email data, illustrating that generic NLP preprocessing can itself materially affect downstream annotation.

limitations: The pilot contains only 54 messages and 310 sentences.
Messages were deliberately selected for varied request and commitment phenomena rather than forming a representative random sample of workplace email.
Messages longer than 11 sentences were excluded.
All three annotators were the paper's authors, limiting independence from guideline design.
The task omitted organizational hierarchy and sender-recipient relationship information that coders themselves identified as relevant.
The annotations did not provide complete conversation-thread context or quoted-message adjacency information.
Strength categories showed low agreement, especially for commitments, and the authors planned to replace or supplement strength with conditionality and explicitness.
Email preprocessing and sentence segmentation contained non-trivial errors.
The study measures human annotation reliability and does not evaluate an automatic request or commitment classifier.
raw_claims: The pilot corpus contains 54 Enron messages and 310 sentences.
Three coders independently annotated the presence and strength of requests and commitments.
Agreement was highest for single-recipient messages and lowest for closed-group messages.
Conditional offers caused a large share of commitment-presence disagreements.
Implicit meeting requests were a recurring source of coder disagreement.
Organizational relationships can change how strongly a request is interpreted.
Coder flags indicated a sentence-segmentation error rate of at least 10% in the pilot data.
The authors planned to refine the scheme toward conditionality and explicitness rather than relying only on strength.
